blocks.text: “Thanks, and thanks, and thanks again for your sweet letter. It was so nice to be able to tell you and to have your sympathy.

“My dear, everything happens all at once. As the old saying goes, it never rains, it pours. How true the old sayings are! I will be twenty in September. Yet until today, I had never had a marriage proposal—not a real one. And today I have had three! Just imagine that! THREE proposals in one day! Isn’t it awful? I feel sorry, really and truly sorry, for two of the poor men. Oh, Mina, I am so happy that I do not know what to do with myself. And three proposals! But for goodness’ sake, do not tell any of the other girls. Otherwise, they will get all sorts of wild ideas. If they do not get at least six proposals on their very first day at home, they will imagine that they have been hurt and treated without respect. Some girls are so proud of themselves! You and I, Mina dear, are engaged to be married. Soon we will settle down quietly and sensibly as old married women. So we can look down on that kind of foolish pride. Well, I must tell you about the three proposals. But you must keep it a secret from everyone, dear, except Jonathan, of course. You will tell him, because I would certainly tell Arthur if I were in your place. A woman ought to tell her husband everything—don’t you think so, dear? And I must be fair. Men like women—and certainly their wives—to be just as honest and fair as they are. And I am afraid that women are not always as fair as they should be. Well, my dear, the first man came just before lunch. I have told you about him before. He is Dr. John Seward, the man who runs the mental hospital. He has a strong jaw and a fine forehead. On the outside he seemed very calm, but he was nervous all the same. Clearly, he had been training himself carefully in all kinds of small ways to stay calm, and he remembered to do them. Even so, he almost sat down on his silk hat! Men do not usually do that when they are truly calm. Then, while he was trying to look relaxed, he kept playing with a small doctor’s knife in a way that almost made me scream. He spoke to me very honestly and directly, Mina. He told me how much he loved me, even though he had known me for such a short time. He told me how wonderful his life would be if I were with him to help him and make him happy. He was about to tell me how unhappy he would be if I did not love him. But when he saw me cry, he stopped. He said he was being cruel and would not add to my present trouble. Then he paused and asked if I could learn to love him in time. When I shook my head, his hands shook. Then, after hesitating a little, he asked me if I already loved someone else. He asked this very kindly. He said he did not want to force my secret out of me. He only wanted to know because if a woman’s heart was still free, a man might still have hope. Then, Mina, I felt it was my duty to tell him that there was someone else. I only told him that much. Then he stood up, looking very strong and very serious. He took both of my hands in his and said he hoped I would be happy. He also said that if I ever needed a friend, I must count him as one of my best friends. Oh, Mina dear, I cannot stop crying! You must excuse this letter for being covered with tear stains. Having a man ask to marry you is very nice, of course. But it is not a happy thing at all when you know that a poor man truly loves you, and you have to watch him walk away looking completely heartbroken. And it is sad to know that, no matter what he says right now, you are going completely out of his life. My dear, I must stop writing for now. I feel so sad, even though I am so happy.

“Arthur has just left. I feel happier now than when I stopped writing earlier, so I can go on telling you about the day. Well, my dear, the second man came after lunch. He is such a nice man, an American from Texas. He looks so young and full of energy that it seems almost impossible that he has traveled to so many places and had so many adventures. I understand how poor Desdemona in Shakespeare’s play felt when such an exciting stream of stories was poured into her ear, even by a Black man. I suppose we women are so easily frightened that we think a brave man will save us from our fears, and so we marry him. Now I know what I would do if I were a man and wanted to make a girl love me. No, I do not! After all, Mr. Morris told us his exciting stories, and Arthur never told any, and yet— My dear, I am getting ahead of my story. Mr. Quincey P. Morris found me alone. It seems that a man always manages to find a girl alone. No, that is not true either! Arthur tried twice to find a chance to be alone with me, even while I was helping him as much as I could. I am not ashamed to admit that now. First, I must tell you that Mr. Morris does not always use slang—that is, informal American expressions. He never uses slang when he speaks to strangers or in front of them, because he is really well educated and has wonderful manners. However, he noticed that it made me laugh to hear him talk in American slang. So whenever I was there, and there was no one around to be shocked, he said such funny things. My dear, I think he must invent it all himself, because it fits so perfectly with everything else he says. But that is how slang works. I do not know if I will ever use slang myself. I do not know if Arthur likes it, because I have never heard him use any yet. Well, Mr. Morris sat down beside me. He tried to look as happy and cheerful as he could, but I could still see that he was very nervous. He took my hand in his, and said in a very sweet voice:—
